newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea Finance Ministry seen fighting reform plan.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea Finance Ministry seen fighting reform plan.

text.p: The mandarins at South Korea's powerful Finance Ministry would likely fight a presidential panel's proposed financial reforms because many would curtail their clout, economists said on Monday.

The Presidential Commission for Financial Reform has proposed ending the Finance Ministry's roles in supervising and licencing the financial industry and in formulating monetary policies. Those proposals are part of a broader reform plan.

"Those functions are the heart of the Finance Ministry's power," said Lee Phil-san, economic professor at Korea University. "I have no doubt the Finance Ministry will oppose proposals that deprive officials there of their authority."

A ministry official told reporters on Monday that Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik, who last week pledged to implement reform measures, said in a luncheon with senior ministry officials that the panel's proposals could be revised.
A different Finance Ministry official said: "We understand the principles recommended by the commission. But some of them need to be further discussed as they are lacking."
"We cannot accept 100 percent of the proposals," he added.

One area of disagreement was likely to be over a panel recommendation to unify the three agencies that now oversee the banking, securities and insurance industries and put the new watchdog body under the prime minister's direct control.
The president should grant ministerial rank to the new agency's head, the panel recommended.
At present, the Finance Minister appoints the heads of the Office of Bank Supervision, the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board, and they report to him.

In another clash with the Finance Ministry, the 31-member commission also recommended enhancing the independence of the central Bank of Korea by outlining its authority to design and implement monetary and inflation policies.
The central bank governor should chair the Monetary Board, which decides monetary policies, the commission recommended.

The ministry has played a leading role in setting monetary policies and has tried, critics argue, to control the central bank. Some cynics have described the central bank as a "branch office" of the Finance Ministry.
The presidential commission is due to formally present its proposals to the president by the end of May.
After that, the Finance Ministry would draft implementing legislation, which Kang promised last week to introduce to a special parliamentary session in June.
"The finance minister will have sessions of deep discussions with ministry officials," said Kim Jun-il, senior counselor to Finance Minister.
Economists said the commission plan was aimed at limiting the Finance Ministry's functions to policy-making.

Since the ministry was merged with the former Economic Planning Board into the Ministry of Finance and the Economy in 1994, the ministry has exerted too much influence over the economy, economists said.

"I believe the commission has come up with such drastic measures because the Finance Ministry has lost its ability to introduce financial reforms," said an economist at the Korea Development Institute, who asked not to be named.
The institute is run by the Finance Ministry.
"It has become too powerful and bureaucratic," he said.
